# NHTS data cleaning and variable construction

This document prepares a **person-level analysis dataset** by combining the
NHTS person and trip files, checking travel distances, selecting eligible adult
travellers, and recoding variables for subsequent descriptive statistics and
regression analysis.

**Path convention:** The relative file paths in this document assume that the
R working directory is the project's `R/` folder. The prefix `../` moves up to
the project root, where `data/` and `tables/` are stored. Run `# Print the working directory that relative file paths are based on.
# If this displays the project's R/ folder, ../data/raw/ refers to the
# data/raw/ folder one level above it.
getwd()` to
confirm your working directory before executing the document. If you run code
from the project root instead, the relative paths will need adjusting.

**Important:** This workflow calculates each person's unweighted mean of their
recorded trip distances. The person-level survey weight is parsed and retained
for later analysis but is not applied to the mean calculation here.

```{r}
# Load packages for importing, transforming, summarising, and inspecting data.
```

```{r}
library(tidyverse)

# PERSON file: one record is intended to represent one surveyed person.
# Using character columns initially avoids accidental loss of leading zeros
# in household IDs, person IDs, and other categorical survey codes.
# Convert only selected variables to numeric later, after checking their codes.
# Check that the person-level data file exists
# file.exists() returns TRUE if the path can be found.
# stopifnot() stops execution if the condition is FALSE; this prevents a
# confusing read_csv() error when the source file is missing.
stopifnot(file.exists("../data/raw/perv2pub.csv"))

# Read the person-level data
# read_csv() imports the CSV as a tibble (a modern data frame).
# col_character() preserves original codes verbatim rather than guessing types.
# show_col_types = FALSE suppresses the import-type message.
person <- read_csv(
  "../data/raw/perv2pub.csv",
  col_types = cols(.default = col_character()),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

# dim() reports c(number_of_rows, number_of_columns).
# Record these counts to document the size of the raw source data.
# Check the dataset dimensions
dim(person)
```


```{r}
# glimpse() shows variable names, storage types, and sample values.
# Use it to confirm that the file imported correctly before merging.
# Inspect the column structure
glimpse(person)
```


```{r}

# TRIP file: a single person can have multiple rows, one for each trip.
# Keep the household/person keys as character strings so they will match
# the corresponding keys from the person dataset.
# Check that the trip-level data file exists
# Stop immediately if the expected trip CSV cannot be located.
stopifnot(file.exists("../data/raw/tripv2pub.csv"))

# Read the trip-level data
# Import raw trip observations without automatic numeric coercion.
# The trip-distance field TRPMILES will be parsed explicitly in Step 7.
trip <- read_csv(
  "../data/raw/tripv2pub.csv",
  col_types = cols(.default = col_character()),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

# Check the dataset dimensions
dim(trip)
```


```{r}
# Inspect the column structure
glimpse(trip)
```


```{r}
# List the exact variable names expected in the person-level file.
# Define this list BEFORE checking the names; otherwise R would report
# "object 'required_person' not found" in a fresh session.
required_person <- c("HOUSEID", "PERSONID", "R_AGE", "HTPPOPDN", "CNTTDTR", "WORKER", "HHSIZE", "HHVEHCNT", "TRAVDAY", "TDAYDATE", "WTPERFIN")

# %in% compares each requested name with the actual column names.
# The result is a logical vector: TRUE = present, FALSE = missing.
person_check <- required_person %in% names(person)

cat("===== Person-Level Variable Check =====\n")

# data.frame() creates an easy-to-read two-column checking table.
# Each row shows the requested variable and whether it was found.
print(data.frame(
  Variable = required_person,
  Exists = person_check
))

```


```{r}
# List required trip variables BEFORE testing for their presence.
# HOUSEID + PERSONID links trips to the person file; TRIPID identifies a trip.
required_trip <- c("HOUSEID", "PERSONID", "TRIPID", "TRPMILES")

# Apply the same presence check to the trip-level dataset.
trip_check <- required_trip %in% names(trip)

cat("\n===== Trip-Level Variable Check =====\n")
# Print the trip-variable results so missing or misspelled columns
# can be identified before data cleaning starts.
print(data.frame(
  Variable = required_trip,
  Exists = trip_check
))
```


```{r}
# all() is TRUE only when every requested variable was found.
# If either condition fails, stop before calculations that need these fields.
# A successful stopifnot() call normally produces no console output.
# This checks column existence, not data completeness or code validity.
stopifnot(
  all(required_person %in% names(person)),
  all(required_trip %in% names(trip))
)
```


```{r}
# ==================================================
# Step 7: Validate trip distances
# ==================================================

# mutate() creates or replaces columns while keeping other columns.
# parse_double() converts the original text distance to a numeric variable.
# Invalid nonnumeric text is converted to NA with a parsing warning.
# Numeric special codes, including negatives, are NOT removed here.
trip <- trip %>% mutate( miles = parse_double(TRPMILES))

# Summarize the overall distribution
# summary() returns the minimum, quartiles, median, mean, and maximum
# (and NA information) for a numeric column. Unusual negative numbers
# should be investigated against the dataset documentation.
summary(trip$miles)
```


```{r}
# Inspect the original values and codes
# count() tabulates each distinct original value or special code.
# sort = TRUE orders the most common values first; compare them with the
# parsed values before deciding what counts as a valid trip distance.
trip %>% count(TRPMILES, sort = TRUE)
```


```{r}
# Count invalid or unusual values
# Summarise the quality of the full trip table in one row.
# n() counts rows; is.na() finds missing parsed values.
# na.rm = TRUE stops missing values from contaminating a logical count.
# is.finite() excludes NA, NaN, Inf, and -Inf.
# Here, distance zero is accepted as nonnegative; negative distances fail.
trip %>%
  summarise(
    total_trips = n(),
    missing_value = sum(is.na(miles)),
    negative_distance = sum(
      miles < 0,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    zero_distance = sum(
      miles == 0,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    valid_distance = sum(
      is.finite(miles) & miles >= 0
    )
  )
```


```{r}
# Identify the specific negative-distance codes
# filter() keeps only rows meeting the stated condition.
# Counting original strings shows which negative numeric codes need review.
# It does NOT delete these rows from the original trip dataset.
trip %>%
  filter(miles < 0) %>%
  count(TRPMILES)
```

```{r}
# ==================================================
# Step 8: Validate dataset keys
# ==================================================

# Person table: one row per person
# The combined HOUSEID + PERSONID columns are intended to identify a person.
# anyDuplicated() returns 0 if there is no duplicate key, otherwise the
# position of the first repeated key. A nonzero result requires investigation.
anyDuplicated(person[c("HOUSEID", "PERSONID")])

# Trip table: each person may have multiple trips
# However, the composite key for each trip must be unique
# HOUSEID + PERSONID + TRIPID should identify a unique trip record.
# A person may legitimately have multiple trips, but their full trip keys
# should not be duplicated.
anyDuplicated(trip[c("HOUSEID", "PERSONID", "TRIPID")])

# Check for trips without a matching person record
# anti_join() returns trip rows without a matching household/person pair
# in the person table. It is a diagnostic and does not modify 'trip'.
# A large unmatched count could signal key-format or source-data problems.
unmatched_trips <- trip %>% anti_join( person, by = c("HOUSEID", "PERSONID"))

# Number of trip rows with no matched person record.
nrow(unmatched_trips)

# Count trips for each person
# Group all trips belonging to the same person.
# group_by() creates one group per HOUSEID + PERSONID pair.
# n() returns the number of trip rows in each group.
# .groups = "drop" produces an ungrouped summary tibble.
trip_counts <- trip %>%
  group_by(HOUSEID, PERSONID) %>%
  summarise(
    # n() includes every recorded trip row, even one with an invalid distance.
    # We retain the raw count to check person-level trip consistency later.
    n_trips = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```


```{r}
# Inspect the results
# head() displays the first six rows by default; it is only a preview.
head(trip_counts)
```


```{r}
# Count unique respondents with recorded trips
# Count how many unique household/person pairs have at least one trip.
# This number is not necessarily the number of all surveyed persons.
nrow(trip_counts)
```

```{r}
# ==================================================
# Step 9: Calculate mean trip distance for each person
# ==================================================

# Unit of analysis changes here: many trip rows become one row per person.
# The outcome mean_trip_miles is a simple arithmetic mean of that person's
# trip distances, not a survey-weighted or distance-weighted average.
# This rule requires ALL observed distances for that person to be valid.
trip_summary <- trip %>%
  group_by(HOUSEID, PERSONID) %>%
  summarise(
    # Count the trips recorded for this person
    n_trips = n(),

    # Check whether all recorded trip distances are valid
    # all() returns TRUE only when every distance is finite and >= 0.
    # Missing values and negative special codes cause this flag to be FALSE.
    all_distances_valid = all(
      is.finite(miles) & miles >= 0
    ),

    # Calculate the mean only if every trip distance is valid
    # if / else creates a mean only for a person with fully valid trip data.
    # NA_real_ is a missing value explicitly stored as a numeric (double).
    mean_trip_miles = if (all_distances_valid) {
      mean(miles)
    } else {
      NA_real_
    },

    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Inspect the newly created summary table
# Confirm that each row represents one person and that the new fields
# n_trips, all_distances_valid, and mean_trip_miles have appropriate types.
glimpse(trip_summary)
```


```{r}
# Check the results
# Audit the person-level trip summary before joining it to the person file.
# The zero_mean total counts people whose valid recorded trips average zero.
trip_summary %>%
  summarise(
    n_persons = n(),
    invalid_persons = sum(!all_distances_valid),
    valid_persons = sum(all_distances_valid),
    zero_mean = sum(
      mean_trip_miles == 0,
      na.rm = TRUE
    )
  )
```

```{r}
# ==================================================
# Step 10: Merge person data with trip summaries
# ==================================================

# left_join() keeps ALL rows from the person file (left table).
# Matching person-level trip summaries are added where keys correspond.
# People with no recorded trips receive NA for new trip-summary fields.
# relationship = "one-to-one" asks dplyr to enforce unique join matches.
person_day <- person %>%
  left_join(
    trip_summary,
    by = c("HOUSEID", "PERSONID"),
    relationship = "one-to-one"
  )

# Compare the number of rows before and after the left join.
# Equal row counts alone do not prove perfect matches, so key and
# missing-value checks elsewhere in the workflow remain important.
# Confirm that the join neither adds nor removes people
nrow(person_day)
nrow(person)

stopifnot(
  nrow(person_day) == nrow(person)
)
```


```{r}
# Inspect a sample of records
# select() keeps the listed columns solely for this preview.
# head(10) shows how the linked trip summaries appear beside person fields;
# the full person_day dataset still contains all original columns.
person_day %>%
  select(
    HOUSEID, PERSONID,
    R_AGE, HTPPOPDN,
    n_trips, mean_trip_miles
  ) %>%
  head(10)
```


```{r}
# ==================================================
# Step 11: Check consistency of trip counts
# ==================================================

# CNTTDTR records the reported daily trip count in the person dataset.
# parse_integer() converts that original character value to an integer.
# coalesce(n_trips, 0L) replaces missing joined trip counts with zero;
# the 'L' suffix marks 0L as an integer rather than a double.
person_day <- person_day %>%
  mutate(
    reported_trips = parse_integer(CNTTDTR),

    recorded_trips = coalesce(
      n_trips, 0L
    )
  )

# Identify respondents with mismatched trip counts
# Keep rows where the reported trip count is missing or differs from
# the number of trip rows that were actually found in the trip file.
# This creates a diagnostic table; the main dataset is NOT filtered here.
mismatch <- person_day %>%
  filter(
    is.na(reported_trips) |
    recorded_trips != reported_trips
  )

# Count respondents with mismatched trip counts
# Print the number of mismatched people for the audit log.
nrow(mismatch)
```


```{r}
# Count respondents with no recorded trips
# Compare the full person sample with the subset having trip records.
# These categories should add up to the number of rows in person_day.
person_day %>%
  summarise(
    all_persons = n(),
    with_trips = sum(recorded_trips > 0),
    without_trips = sum(recorded_trips == 0)
  )
```

```{r}
# ==================================================
# Step 12: Select adult respondents
# ==================================================

# Convert R_AGE from its imported text representation to numeric age.
# inspect the summary below for missing, negative, or special-coded values;
# those values must be interpreted using the NHTS variable documentation.
person_day <- person_day %>%
  mutate(
    age = parse_double(R_AGE)
  )

# Inspect the age distribution
# Review the minimum, quartiles, maximum, and missing ages before filtering.
summary(person_day$age)
```


```{r}
# Count missing age values
# sum(TRUE/FALSE) counts TRUE values because TRUE is treated as 1.
# This reports how many people have an unavailable parsed age.
sum(is.na(person_day$age))

# Keep respondents aged 18 or older
# Adults are defined as age >= 18 for this research question.
# Rows with NA age do not satisfy the condition and are dropped by filter().
adult <- person_day %>%
  filter(age >= 18)

# Count the remaining respondents
nrow(adult)
```

```{r}
# ==================================================
# Step 13: Select adults with recorded trips
# ==================================================

# First count adults with and without recorded trips
# Make a frequency table for adult respondents with or without trips.
# The new column name has_trip is a logical TRUE/FALSE indicator.
adult %>%
  count(
    has_trip = recorded_trips > 0
  )

# Keep only respondents with recorded trips
# Limit analysis to adults who actually made at least one recorded trip.
# Respondents with zero trips cannot contribute a personal mean trip distance.
traveller <- adult %>%
  filter(recorded_trips > 0)
```


```{r}
# Print the adult traveller sample size after this exclusion.
nrow(traveller)
```

### Run the code

```{r}
# ==================================================
# Step 14: Exclude people with invalid trip distances
# ==================================================

# First count people with invalid trip distances
# Review the TRUE/FALSE counts for the person-level distance validity flag.
# TRUE means every trip distance was finite and nonnegative;
# FALSE indicates at least one invalid distance for that person.
traveller %>%
  count(all_distances_valid)
```


```{r}
# Keep people whose recorded trip distances are all valid
# Exclude entire persons (not individual trip rows) if any recorded
# trip distance is invalid, following the rule created in Step 9.
# This is a strict complete-distance criterion and may reduce the sample.
complete_distance <- traveller %>%
  filter(all_distances_valid)

nrow(complete_distance)

# Recheck whether mean trip distances are valid
# A properly constructed complete-distance subset should have no NA
# values in mean_trip_miles. The expected result is zero.
sum(
  is.na(complete_distance$mean_trip_miles)
)
```


```{r}
# ==================================================
# Step 15: Keep valid population-density categories
# ==================================================

# Inspect the distribution of original population-density codes
# Inspect actual density codes before deciding which categories are valid.
# Leading zeros matter because HTPPOPDN was imported as a character field.
complete_distance %>%
  count(HTPPOPDN, sort = TRUE)
```


```{r}
# Define the eight valid category codes
# sprintf("%02d", 1:8) creates "01", "02", ... , "08".
# %02d means a width of two digits with a leading zero when needed.
# Verify these exact codes against the source data and codebook.
valid_density_codes <- sprintf(
  "%02d", 1:8
)

valid_density_codes

# Keep records with valid population-density codes
# %in% retains people whose original population-density code belongs
# to the eight permitted categories. Other codes and NA are excluded.
known_density <- complete_distance %>%
  filter(
    HTPPOPDN %in% valid_density_codes
  )

nrow(known_density)
```

```{r}
# Display all permitted density codes as an additional diagnostic.
# This repeats the category-code construction used above.
sprintf("%02d", 1:8)
```

```{r}
# ==================================================
# Step 16: Inspect and clean the core control variables
# ==================================================

# Convert three control variables to numeric representations.
# hh_size is household size; vehicles is the household vehicle count;
# person_weight is the respondent-level survey weight.
# parse_double() may return NA for nonnumeric codes; later filters handle
# some invalid values, but the output distributions should be inspected.
known_density <- known_density %>%
  mutate(
    hh_size = parse_double(HHSIZE),
    vehicles = parse_double(HHVEHCNT),
    person_weight = parse_double(WTPERFIN)
  )

# Distribution of employment status
# Frequency table of the original WORKER codes.
# Check that expected codes "01" and "02" actually occur in the data.
known_density %>%
  count(WORKER)
```


```{r}
# Household size
# Inspect household size. Values <= 0 are not acceptable and
# will be removed during the final eligibility filter.
summary(known_density$hh_size)
```


```{r}
# Number of household vehicles
# Inspect household vehicle ownership. Negative values often indicate
# special missing/unknown codes rather than a real number of cars.
summary(known_density$vehicles)
```


```{r}
# Day of the week for the travel survey
# Tabulate day-of-week codes before converting them to labelled factors.
# The code below assumes two-character codes from "01" through "07".
known_density %>%
  count(TRAVDAY)
```


```{r}
# Person-level survey weights
# A valid survey weight should be finite and greater than zero.
# This script retains a weight for future modelling, but does not yet
# apply survey weights to trip means or summary statistics.
summary(known_density$person_weight)
```


```{r}
# Check the regional control variable
# Inspect region identifiers; factor() in Step 17 will represent
# these as categories, not as numerical distances between regions.
known_density %>%
  count(CENSUS_R)
```


```{r}
# Check the survey date codes
# Inspect survey-date / survey-period codes.
# Step 17 preserves each distinct observed code as a factor level.
known_density %>%
  count(TDAYDATE)
```


```{r}
# Apply the final eligibility rules for core control variables.
# filter() combines these comma-separated conditions with logical AND:
# employment code is valid, household size positive, vehicle count
# nonnegative, survey weekday recognised, and person weight positive/finite.
# Rows failing any condition (including NA comparisons) are removed.
# Note: people with mismatched trip counts were flagged earlier, not excluded.
analysis_data <- known_density %>%
  filter(
    WORKER %in% c("01", "02"),
    hh_size > 0,
    vehicles >= 0,
    TRAVDAY %in% sprintf("%02d", 1:7),
    is.finite(person_weight),
    person_weight > 0
  )

# Check the number of complete observations available for analysis.
nrow(analysis_data)
```

```{r}
# ==================================================
# Step 17: Recode variables
# ==================================================

# Create analysis-ready variables without deleting their source columns.
# factor() stores categorical values as levels; the order of levels can
# affect which category is used as the reference in regression models.
# The recodes assume the original survey-code definitions are correct.
analysis_data <- analysis_data %>%
  mutate(

    # 1. Main independent variable: census-tract population density
    # The factor contains eight ordered-in-list categories "01" to "08".
    # This is a categorical predictor: no numeric distance is inferred
    # between adjacent population-density bands by factor().
    density_band = factor(
      HTPPOPDN,
      levels = sprintf("%02d", 1:8)
    ),

    # 2. Employment status
    # Assign readable text labels to the two permitted original codes.
    # Because "01" is listed first, 'worker' is the default reference level
    # in a treatment-coded regression unless relevelled later.
    worker = factor(
      WORKER,
      levels = c("01", "02"),
      labels = c("worker", "not_worker")
    ),

    # 3. Household vehicle ownership groups
    # Use case_when() to combine numeric vehicle counts into three groups:
    # no vehicles, exactly one, and two or more. The factor's first level
    # ("0") becomes the reference category by default.
    car_group = factor(
      case_when(
        vehicles == 0 ~ "0",
        vehicles == 1 ~ "1",
        vehicles >= 2 ~ "2+"
      ),
      levels = c("0", "1", "2+")
    ),

    # 4. Day of the week for the travel survey
    # Map the seven source weekday codes onto named days.
    # Confirm the original 01=Sunday ... 07=Saturday mapping in the codebook;
    # if these source codes differ, all resulting day names would be wrong.
    day_of_week = factor(
      TRAVDAY,
      levels = sprintf("%02d", 1:7),
      labels = c(
        "Sunday",
        "Monday",
        "Tuesday",
        "Wednesday",
        "Thursday",
        "Friday",
        "Saturday"
      )
    ),

    # 5. Survey period
    # Preserve observed survey-date identifiers as discrete categories.
    # This is not a Date object; no chronological arithmetic is performed.
    survey_period = factor(TDAYDATE),

    # 6. Census region
    # Treat census region as a categorical regional control variable.
    census_region = factor(CENSUS_R),

    # 7. Convert miles to kilometres
    # One mile equals exactly 1.609344 kilometres.
    # This changes measurement units, not the people included in analysis.
    mean_trip_km = mean_trip_miles * 1.609344,

    # 8. Precompute a log-transformed version
    # log1p(x) computes ln(1 + x), allowing x = 0 (result = 0).
    # Here x is measured in miles; the log of km would be numerically
    # different. Keep the choice of outcome units consistent in reporting.
    log_mean_trip = log1p(mean_trip_miles)
  )

# Preview the first six rows of the newly recoded variables.
# The original dataset is unchanged by select() and head(); they are used
# solely to display a compact subset for inspection.
# Also review factor frequencies and NA counts before regression.
head(select(analysis_data,
    density_band,
    worker,
    car_group,
    day_of_week,
    survey_period,
    census_region,
    mean_trip_km,
    log_mean_trip))
```


```{r}
# ==================================================
# Final check A: Sample sizes
# ==================================================

# Number of eligible adult travellers
# nrow() is the current analysis sample size, after all exclusions.
# A person-level analysis should have one row per unique person key.
nrow(analysis_data)

# Number of distinct households
# n_distinct() counts unique household identifiers; multiple people
# from the same household count as one household.
n_distinct(analysis_data$HOUSEID)

# Number of distinct people
# Count unique combinations, not unique PERSONID values alone.
# Person identifiers may be reused across different households.
n_distinct(
  analysis_data$HOUSEID,
  analysis_data$PERSONID
)

# Check for duplicate records for the same person
# Expected output is 0. A nonzero result means the person-level
# analysis dataset contains duplicate household/person keys.
anyDuplicated(
  analysis_data[c("HOUSEID", "PERSONID")]
)
```


```{r}
# ==================================================
# Final check B: Dependent variable
# ==================================================

# Main dependent variable: the mean distance per recorded trip for each
# eligible adult, expressed in miles. Inspect distribution and extremes.
summary(analysis_data$mean_trip_miles)

# Count missing dependent-variable values; expected to be zero after
# the complete-distance restriction in Step 14.
sum(is.na(analysis_data$mean_trip_miles))

# Check for impossible negative mean distances; expected count is zero.
sum(analysis_data$mean_trip_miles < 0)

# Zero means are allowed by this workflow; record how frequent they are.
sum(analysis_data$mean_trip_miles == 0)

# Quantiles locate the 25th, 50th, 75th, 95th, and 99th percentiles.
# They are useful for detecting a long right tail in trip distances.
# na.rm = TRUE ignores missing data when calculating these cutoffs.
quantile(
  analysis_data$mean_trip_miles,
  probs = c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.95, 0.99),
  na.rm = TRUE
)
```


```{r}
# ==================================================
# Final check C: Population density
# ==================================================

# Show the number of analysed people and distinct households
# in each population-density band. Very small groups can produce
# unstable model estimates and should be reported.
analysis_data %>%
  group_by(density_band) %>%
  summarise(
    persons = n(),
    households = n_distinct(HOUSEID),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```



```{r}
# ==================================================
# Final check D: Feasibility of interaction analysis
# ==================================================

# Cross-tabulate density groups against vehicle-ownership groups.
# pivot_wider() converts the long counts into one column per car group.
# values_fill = 0 fills absent group combinations with explicit zeros.
# Empty/small cells may limit interaction-model precision.
analysis_data %>%
  count(
    density_band,
    car_group
  ) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = car_group,
    values_from = n,
    values_fill = 0
  )
```


```{r}
# ==================================================
# Final check E: Sample selection flow
# ==================================================

# Build a transparent sample-flow table for methods reporting.
# Each row corresponds to a sequential sample-selection checkpoint.
# The list of remaining_n entries MUST follow the same order as step.
# These are counts of people (not trip rows).
sample_flow <- tibble(
  step = c(
    "All respondents",
    "Adults aged 18+",
    "Adult travellers",
    "Complete trip distances",
    "Valid population density",
    "Valid core covariates"
  ),

  remaining_n = c(
    nrow(person),
    nrow(adult),
    nrow(traveller),
    nrow(complete_distance),
    nrow(known_density),
    nrow(analysis_data)
  )
) %>%
  mutate(
    # lag() shifts the previous stage's remaining count down by one row.
    # Current excluded_n = previous_remaining - current_remaining.
    # default = first(...) makes the initial excluded count equal to zero.
    excluded_n = lag(
      remaining_n,
      default = first(remaining_n)
    ) - remaining_n,

    # Calculate the share of the original person sample retained at
    # each stage. round(..., 2) keeps two decimal places for reporting.
    retained_percent = round(
      100 * remaining_n / first(remaining_n),
      2
    )
  )

# Display the full sample flow, including exclusions at each stage.
# Save this table later so the numbers can be used in the report.
print(sample_flow)
```

```{r}
# ==================================================
# Save outputs
# ==================================================

# Output paths are now aligned with the input-path convention above:
# ../data/processed and ../tables are located in the project root.
# This assumes the current working directory is the project's R/ folder.
# If you run from a different directory, check getwd() first.
# Create the processed directory if it does not exist
dir.create(
  "../data/processed",
  # recursive = TRUE can create missing parent directories.
  # showWarnings = FALSE avoids a warning when the folder already exists.
  recursive = TRUE,
  showWarnings = FALSE
)

# Make a separate output folder for tables used in the report.
dir.create(
  "../tables",
  recursive = TRUE,
  showWarnings = FALSE
)

# saveRDS() preserves R-specific types such as factors and numeric columns.
# Later, readRDS() can restore analysis_data without re-importing CSV text.
# Save in the native R data format
saveRDS(
  analysis_data,
  "../data/processed/analysis_data.rds"
)

# write_csv() creates a portable, human-readable table, but factor
# level metadata is not retained as it is in an RDS file.
# Also save as CSV for manual inspection
write_csv(
  analysis_data,
  "../data/processed/analysis_data.csv"
)

# Export the sample-flow audit, including counts and percentages,
# for use in the methodology and data-cleaning section of the paper.
# Save the sample selection table
write_csv(
  sample_flow,
  "../tables/sample_flow.csv"
)
```
